results.title: Mimrr: Features, Pricing & Alternatives for Dev Teams
results.content:
No dependable public pricing table makes budget comparison difficult.
 Product access appears sales-led rather than immediately self-serve.
 The public site provides limited technical detail about model architecture, supported languages and exact feature boundaries.
 Claims about private deployment and data isolation should be confirmed in architecture diagrams and contract terms.
 Connecting code, tickets and chat creates a broad permission surface that should be minimized carefully.
 Generated documentation can be fluent but wrong, especially around runtime behavior and hidden operational constraints.
 Generated unit tests may reinforce the current implementation instead of testing the intended contract.
 AI pull-request comments can add noise unless teams tune scope and severity. [...] ### Can Mimrr run on-premises?

Mimrr advertises VPC and on-premises readiness. Buyers should verify the exact architecture, model hosting, update process and support responsibilities for their proposed deployment.

### Does Mimrr train on customer code?

Mimrr says it never trains on customer data and does not connect to third-party AI solutions. Treat that as a vendor claim to confirm through technical and contractual diligence.

### How much does Mimrr cost?

The current site is demo-led and does not expose a dependable public plan table. Ask for a quote covering users, repositories, usage, deployment, integrations, onboarding and support.

### What happened to the Rune extension? [...] Bottom line

## Our Mimrrverdict

Mimrr has a useful premise for teams whose code, tickets and decisions live in separate systems: connect that context and automate the repetitive handoffs. Its privacy-oriented deployment story is potentially differentiating, but the sparse technical and pricing detail means the right buying motion is a tightly scoped pilot with explicit security, accuracy and export requirements.

results.title: The 3 R’s to Handling Customer Complaints
results.content:
The first R in my formula stands for the word RESPECT.  It is critical that you or your employee show respect to the customer.  You can do this by listening and letting the customer vent their feelings and frustration. The longer you are able to listen, the better. Sincerely, use cushion statements to ease the frustration level of the customer.  A cushion statement is anything you say or do that shows the customer you empathize with their concern.  Some examples would be: “You are right to feel concerned” or “That must be frustrating” or “I can appreciate your concern.” Then let them vent. [...] The next R stands for the word RAPPORT. You can develop rapport with the person by sincerely apologizing for any trouble that happened to the person who experienced the problem. One way you could say this is: “Mr. Jones, I want apologize for any trouble this has caused you”. Then thank them for bringing this concern to your attention.

The third R stands for RESOLVE. Here is where you resolve the situation to the best of your ability. One question you could ask is: “What action would you like us to take?” Many times the complaining person’s idea of a resolution is much less than you would think. The key here is to take action and if possible, resolve the problem.
